objective: Know that input tokens and generated output tokens share one context window, so a long prompt leaves less room for the answer.

original.hint: Consider what the model is reading while it generates the last sentence of a long reply.
original.question: Within a single request, the context window must accommodate:
options: Only the input prompt
Both the input tokens and the output tokens together
Only the model's output
Neither input nor output
original.explanation: One window covers the whole request: system prompt, messages, tool definitions and documents, plus every token the model generates in reply. So a prompt that nearly fills the window leaves almost no room for an answer, and generation stops early - which is why you size a request with headroom for the output limit you set. Input-only and output-only are both wrong for the same reason: the model attends to the prompt and its own partial output as one continuous sequence.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Scope the shared-budget rule to the stated decoder-only setup rather than every possible architecture/provider. Remove the guaranteed early-stop claim because oversized requests can be rejected or limited before generation.
evidence: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows

objective: Define hallucination as fluent output that is factually wrong or fabricated, and separate it from other LLM failure modes.

original.hint: Ask what is wrong in a hallucination: the shape of the output, or what it claims.
original.question: In the context of LLMs, what is a 'hallucination'?
options: When the model refuses to answer
When the model produces fluent, confident-sounding text that is factually wrong or fabricated
When the model runs out of tokens mid-sentence
When the model repeats the same word forever
original.explanation: A hallucination is content that reads as fact but is not supported by the sources or by reality, and it is hard to spot precisely because the text is fluent and specific. Truncation, looping repetition and refusal are separate failure modes where the output is visibly wrong; a hallucination looks right. The name is a metaphor: mechanically the model is continuing the text with likely tokens, and nothing in that process checks a claim against a source.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Shorten the definition without making fluency/confidence universal requirements. Avoid claiming that every model system lacks retrieval or verification mechanisms.
evidence: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf

objective: State what referential integrity guarantees: no foreign-key value without a matching row.

original.hint: Ask which writes the database starts refusing once the constraint exists.
original.question: What does "referential integrity" ensure?
options: Every foreign key value points to an existing row
Every column is indexed
All data is encrypted
Queries always run fast
original.explanation: Referential integrity means every foreign-key value matches an existing row in the referenced table: the database rejects an insert or update pointing at nothing, and blocks or cascades a delete that would orphan rows. Indexing, encryption and query speed are separate properties - Postgres does not even index the referencing column automatically, so integrity and performance are decisions you make separately.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Correct the every-value statement for nullable keys and acknowledge referential actions beyond blocking/cascading. Specify a single-column key to avoid composite MATCH semantics.
evidence: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-FK

objective: Recognize a self join as joining a table to itself under two aliases.

original.hint: Ask what the word 'self' has to refer to here, then check which option matches that reading.
original.question: A "self join" is:
options: Joining a table to itself (e.g. employees to their managers)
Joining two unrelated databases
A join that never returns rows
A join without a condition
original.explanation: A self join lists one table twice under different aliases - FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id - because without the aliases no column reference could say which copy it means. It matches rows of a table to other rows of the same table, which is how hierarchies are queried. Joining two separate databases is a different problem, and a join with no condition is a cross join.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Keep the same-table/two-role definition and remove the broad equation of any no-condition join with cross join. Demonstrate inner and left self joins with synthetic VALUES only.
evidence: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-TABLE-ALIASES

objective: Recognize a repeating group under the conventional introductory first-normal-form guideline.

original.hint: Look at what a single column may hold, not at how many tables the schema has.
original.question: First normal form (1NF) requires that:
options: Every column holds a single atomic value (no repeating groups/arrays)
There are no foreign keys
Every table has exactly one column
Data is denormalized
original.explanation: 1NF asks that a column hold one value per row rather than a repeating group - not tags packed into a comma-separated string, and not phone1/phone2/phone3 columns - because you cannot filter, join or constrain part of a field reliably. Foreign keys, table count and denormalization are unrelated to it. A Postgres array or jsonb column is a deliberate exception, taken when the value is always read and written as a whole.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Use an explicit conventional-design example rather than an absolute ban on every rich SQL value. Remove the claim that arrays/JSON become deliberate 1NF exceptions merely because an application reads/writes them as a whole.
evidence: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/troubleshoot/microsoft-365/microsoft-365-apps/access/database-normalization-description
